findings.title: GitHub user check is skipped whenever no Integration row exists yet
findings.body: The authenticated-user comparison (lines 500-505) only runs after `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` succeeds. The `except Integration.DoesNotExist` branch at 481-482 returns `pipeline.next_step()` without comparing `github_authenticated_user` to anyone. `installation_id` comes from the query string and takes precedence over the bound state (line 448). If the installation webhook has not been processed yet (the user is redirected at the same time the webhook fires) or was never delivered, anyone who supplies that installation_id gets it linked to their org. `build_integration` then fetches the installation with the app JWT. `test_basic_flow` exercises exactly this path with no webhook, so the PR's stated guarantee that the pipeline fails on a user mismatch does not hold. A failed or late webhook should be treated as a failure or verified some other way, not as success.

findings.title: KeyError/500 when existing Integration has no `sender` metadata
findings.body: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes `sender` is always present. `build_integration` only stores it when `state.get("sender")` is truthy, so integrations created through the pipeline flow without a prior webhook, or created before sender tracking, have no `sender`. For such an Integration that has no OrganizationIntegration (for example, a re-install after the org integration was removed), the lookup raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of the friendly error page. Use `.get` and treat missing data as a validation failure or handle it explicitly.

findings.title: OAuth `state` is a deterministic pipeline signature, not a per-session nonce
findings.body: The `state` sent to GitHub and later compared (line 412) is `pipeline.signature`. It is derived from the pipeline's views and is the same for every user and org; the tests reuse the same hard-coded value for two different orgs and users. It is therefore guessable and gives no CSRF or session binding for the OAuth authorize round trip. Anyone can craft a callback URL with their own `code` and the known `state`. The comparison is also a plain `!=` rather than a constant-time compare. For a security fix whose description lists the state check as a protection, use a random, session-bound value.

findings.title: Network/HTTP failures in the token exchange and user lookup are not handled
findings.body: `safe_urlopen(...)` at line 423 is outside the `try`, so connection errors or timeouts raise and produce a 500. `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` at line 434 also performs an HTTP request and can raise on non-2xx responses or network errors; only the missing-`login` case is handled. These GitHub-side failures should yield the same friendly `error(...)` response as the other failure modes the PR describes.

findings.title: Authorize URL query string is built by string interpolation without encoding
findings.body: `client_id`, `state` and `redirect_uri` are interpolated directly into the authorize URL. `redirect_uri` is a full URL containing `:` and `/`, and it is not percent-encoded. It works with GitHub today, but it is fragile, for example with a customized `url-prefix`, and `urlencode` should be used.

findings.title: test_installation_not_found no longer tests the installation-not-found path
findings.body: The test still stubs the installation lookup with a 404. It now sends a bogus `state` (`ddd023d8...`), so the flow ends in the state-mismatch error and asserts the generic "Invalid installation request." message. The `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")` branch in `build_integration` is therefore no longer covered, and the old assertion was silently replaced. The test now passes for a reason unrelated to its name.

findings.title: Only one of the new failure modes (and no success case for an existing Integration) is tested
findings.body: The PR lists three failure causes: user mismatch, state mismatch, and a failed `code` exchange. Only the user mismatch is tested. Nothing covers a wrong `state`, an `access_token` exchange failure, a `/user` response with no `login`, or an Integration that exists with no `sender` metadata. There is also no positive test where the authenticated GitHub user matches `metadata["sender"]["login"]` for a pre-existing Integration. Without these, the new validation can regress, or crash as in the KeyError case, unnoticed.
